bottom_line: You can expect a prompt first reply (median 2.3 hours) and outsiders do get merged—28 distinct first-time authors had PRs merged in the sample. However responsiveness is inconsistent: 55 of 119 outsider PRs were left without any visible response.
summary:
The clearest signal is that outside contributions are accepted and often get a fast initial reaction: 28 first-time PRs by 28 distinct authors were merged out of 119 outsider attempts by 81 people, and the median time to first response was 2.3 hours. This is a real application repository (Home Assistant core) with substantive onboarding: the CONTRIBUTING guide gives a concrete PR process and points to developer documentation and discussion venues.

That positive behaviour sits alongside notable inconsistency. In the sample 55 of 119 outsider threads received no visible response, some PRs were closed dismissively, and many threads show changes requested rather than quick merges. Maintainer comments range from constructive review—"Looks good, but please address the valid bot comments."—to silence, and the bot share is low (≈5.5%), so most interactions are with humans and vary by area and reviewer.
decided_by: 28 pull requests from outside contributors were merged, by 28 different people, out of 119 attempts by 81 people. Of those who got a reply, half heard back within 2.3 hours. 55 attempts got no reply at all and weren't merged.
unknowns: I could not determine how consistently maintainers will help an outsider who is blocked by local setup, failing CI, or other hands-on onboarding problems.

evidence.text: A software project. The repository is the Home Assistant core project (an open-source home automation platform). The merged PRs modify application code, integration components, tests, and CI workflows (not just catalogue entries or a curated list). Examples…

Clear enough to follow. The CONTRIBUTING file gives a clear, actionable route for outsiders: it invites contributions, lists a step-by-step process for proposing code (read PR guidance, fork the repo, write code, ensure tests pass, create a PR against the dev…

Mixed. Some PRs receive substantive review and are merged after feedback (welcoming), while many others are left open with little or no visible response (ignored) or closed without engagement. Overall this shows an active review culture in places…

headline: Worth your time
verdict_line: Outside contributors do get merged here, but about half get no reply, so choose your first change carefully.
numbers_line: Of 119 pull requests from outside contributors (27 May – 31 May 2026), 28 were merged (24%). When a maintainer replied, it was typically within 2.3 hours. 46% sat open with no reply.
first_timer_line: 28 people got their first pull request merged here.
next_step: Best bet: a small change in homeassistant/components, where 26 of 104 outside pull requests were merged.

counted.text: 200 pull requests on GitHub, opened 27 May – 31 May 2026.

70 of them came from 15 people on the project's team and are left out. The team is everyone GitHub shows as an owner, member or collaborator, plus anyone the history shows merging, closing or formally reviewing other people's pull requests. Everyone else is an outside contributor, including people who come back.
11 pull requests opened by bots (dependency updates and the like) are left out. Only a maintainer's reply counts as a reply: not a bot, a CLA check, the author, or a passer-by.

28 pull requests from outside contributors were merged, by 28 different people, out of 119 attempts by 81 people. Of those who got a reply, half heard back within 2.3 hours. 55 attempts got no reply at all and weren't merged.

Only pull requests from outside contributors opened between 14 days and a year ago count, so each has had time for an answer and reflects how the project works now. “Worth your time” needs at least 2 of them merged, from at least 2 different people, with at least 3 in 10 people getting their first pull request merged (once 8 or more have tried), at least 1 in 10 merged, no more than half left without any reply, a typical first reply within 3 weeks, and people actually reviewing what gets merged. “Long shot” is a project that merges some outside work but misses one of those: fewer than 3 in 10 newcomers getting in, fewer than 1 in 10 merged, most left unanswered, very slow first replies, or only one person's work getting in. “Not worth your time” is an archived repository, a mirror, a project with nothing merged or pushed in 90 days, merges nobody reviews, fewer than 1 in 20 outside pull requests merged once at least 20 have been decided, or outside pull requests that are almost all ignored. “Personal project” is someone's own project or a small team's, like a hackathon entry, with nothing from outside ever merged. “A list, not code” is a list or a catalogue of entries, like links or package listings: entries get merged easily, but they aren't code. Anything in between is “Not enough evidence”. These rules are fixed; no AI chooses the verdict.
